title: Strained System: Children's Social Care, regional responses and market failures
label: 28 October 2026 · Children’s social care evidence session
summary: Local government and sector leaders described a children’s social care system under heavy financial strain, rising complexity in children’s needs, problems in the provider market, and delays in registering good homes. They welcomed regional care co‑operatives as helpful for specialist placements and workforce development but warned they are not a quick fix. Key priorities are speeding up registration, better health-education-social care coordination, regulating profit-driven providers, and investing in training, fostering and care-leaver housing.

glossary.definition: A voluntary joint body of local authorities that commissions and develops children’s homes and fostering at regional scale.
The government agency that inspects and registers children’s homes and schools.
Care Quality Commission, the regulator for health and adult social care services.
Integrated Care Board: NHS bodies that plan health services for local areas.
Highly specialist inpatient mental health services for children and adolescents.
When a child is looked after by relatives or family friends instead of the state placing them with strangers.

A proposed legal limit on how much profit providers of children’s care can retain.

chapters.title: Where the system is now
chapters.takeaway: Children’s services face big unfunded costs, rising complexity of needs, and several reforms that will change demand.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Please introduce yourselves and give a snapshot of legislative, financial and supply‑demand pressures.

turns.speaker: Rachael Wardell
turns.text: I lead children’s services in Surrey and represent directors nationally. There’s a big package of reforms—Families First, Best Start, SEND—that will change who needs care. Implementing Families First by March is underway. We’re already seeing pressures on placements and how care is provided.

turns.speaker: Lucy Butler
turns.text: I run the South East Regional Care Cooperative. We’re a voluntary group of 15 of 19 local authorities in the region, working on fostering reforms and sufficiency. We’re a pathfinder alongside Greater Manchester, but this is a decades‑old problem that won’t be fixed overnight.

turns.speaker: Gerald Vernon-Jackson
turns.text: At the LGA I see councils putting in around £1 billion a year into children’s social care with no central funding. Children’s needs are more complex—mental health, exploitation, substance use—while high‑cost placements are rising sharply.

chapters.title: Regional care co‑operatives: potential and limits
chapters.takeaway: RCCs can buy and develop specialist places and train staff at scale, but budgets mostly remain with councils and change will be slow.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Lucy, expand on how your care co‑operative works: funding, sufficiency and cross‑boundary issues.

turns.speaker: Lucy Butler
turns.text: We use a memorandum of understanding with ICBs and provider collaboratives, work sub‑regionally, and have a funding formula paid by member councils. We’re strategic commissioners, not a single pooled budget—directors keep statutory duties so full budget pooling is a big step.

turns.speaker: Lucy Butler
turns.text: We’re focused on joint pathways with health, training for residential staff, and bringing children’s voices in. Sufficiency is complex: many south‑east children live in London and vice versa, so some problems are regional, some national.

turns.speaker: Rachael Wardell
turns.text: RCCs are useful especially for low‑number, high‑need children where one authority can’t justify specialist provision alone. But local connections matter: keeping children near family, school and friends often works better.

turns.speaker: Gerald Vernon-Jackson
turns.text: RCCs can help on the specialist end, but they’re not a quick fix; expect slow change. The number of extremely high‑cost placements rose steeply—some costing tens of thousands a week—and that scale of problem won’t reverse fast.

chapters.title: Market problems, profit and regulation
chapters.takeaway: The provider market is dominated by private equity seeking profit; measures in the Act help but may not be strong enough without early use and further regulation.

turns.speaker: Lord Faulkner of Worcester
turns.text: Will the Children’s Wellbeing and Schools Act market measures fix a fundamentally broken market?

turns.speaker: Gerald Vernon-Jackson
turns.text: Probably not. Many large providers are private‑equity‑backed and profit‑driven. The Act is welcome, but we need more power to regulate those actors effectively.

turns.speaker: Rachael Wardell
turns.text: Measures like a profit cap are welcome, but if used only as a last resort, providers driven by profit will keep moving in. Using the cap early and legislating properly is the realistic route to change.

turns.speaker: Lucy Butler
turns.text: We must avoid unintended consequences: if the market is squeezed suddenly, voluntary or council providers might withdraw. We should remove blockers—registration delays, set‑up costs—so providers we want to keep can grow.

turns.speaker: Lord Barber of Chittlehampton
turns.text: Could providers be pressured to invest profit into staff training instead of taking it out?

turns.speaker: Gerald Vernon-Jackson
turns.text: Good providers will invest; worse providers won’t. RCCs give scope to invest in long‑term, well‑trained residential staff, which helps quality.

turns.speaker: Rachael Wardell
turns.text: Residential staff are low paid but skilled. We need routes for them to develop and be valued; staying in the sector should be an option, not just moving into social work.

chapters.title: Registration delays, unregistered homes and solo placements
chapters.takeaway: Delays in Ofsted registration and planning permissions mean skilled staff and ready homes sit empty, driving use of unregistered or solo placements; capacity and process changes are needed.

turns.speaker: Baroness Watkins of Tavistock
turns.text: Why are councils still using unregistered homes and how is quality supervised in those cases?

turns.speaker: Rachael Wardell
turns.text: Unregistered is now usually a last resort and can be costly. Sometimes a child stabilises in an unregistered setting and moving them would harm them. We try to help providers become registered, but speed matters.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Where are the bottlenecks—Ofsted capacity, planning permission, or registered managers?

turns.speaker: Rachael Wardell
turns.text: All of the above. Ofsted has a surge in applications since supported accommodation became registrable. Planning permission, finding a registered manager and administrative delays all slow registration.

turns.speaker: Gerald Vernon-Jackson
turns.text: I’ve heard of waits up to a year for Ofsted registration. We should set maximum times for registration work so councils and providers can plan.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Would a temporary licence or local authority earned autonomy help?

turns.speaker: Rachael Wardell
turns.text: ADCS has explored temporary registration with Ofsted but finding safe, enforceable conditions has been hard. The principle of 'earned autonomy'—trusted councils doing more—has potential if risk is managed.

turns.speaker: Lucy Butler
turns.text: Two other points: 'solo placements'—one child alone in a home—have risen a lot and are worrying. Also, Ofsted inspects; some very clinical placements need CQC oversight or joint inspection because of health needs.

chapters.title: Fostering, workforce and care leavers
chapters.takeaway: Recruitment targets help but support, training, housing and tailored roles for carers and staff are vital; education and housing for care leavers must improve.

turns.speaker: Baroness Pidgeon
turns.text: What are barriers to recruiting and retaining foster carers, and what is 'end‑to‑end' fostering?

turns.speaker: Gerald Vernon-Jackson
turns.text: Fostering sits behind kinship and prevention. We’ve always recruited foster carers, but we now need more specialist carers as children are older and have more complex needs. Support is the key.

turns.speaker: Rachael Wardell
turns.text: Barriers include economics, housing space, and the complexity of teenage care. Also, many foster families remain caring for young adults via 'staying put', which reduces capacity for new placements.

turns.speaker: Lucy Butler
turns.text: End‑to‑end is the Government term for the whole recruitment and approval process—from first contact to approval. We ran funded regional therapeutic training for foster carers that should be national.

turns.speaker: Baroness Redfern
turns.text: On workforce skill mix: do agency carers have the right skills?

turns.speaker: Rachael Wardell
turns.text: Agency residential staff cover gaps but aren’t always as skilled as permanent staff. High turnover or sickness forces agencies in; that risks quality and sometimes forces a home to close or children to move.

turns.speaker: Baroness Hollins
turns.text: What should the DfE prioritise to improve outcomes for children in care?

turns.speaker: Rachael Wardell
turns.text: Secure education quickly for children entering care. Many arrive with fragmented schooling; the Virtual School and PEPs must be effective so educational loss doesn’t push them into NEET outcomes.

turns.speaker: Gerald Vernon-Jackson
turns.text: Housing for care leavers matters too—solo flats alone often fail. Supporting shared or group living, tenancy skills and links to local networks prevents failures. Responsibility to 25 helps but local housing shortages persist.

turns.speaker: Lord Mohammed of Tinsley
turns.text: You mentioned costs of registration delays—can you provide numbers and where delays are longest?

turns.speaker: Gerald Vernon-Jackson
turns.text: We don’t have the national cost number in front of us but will gather the data on delay costs and geographic patterns for the committee.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you. Any final reflections?

turns.speaker: Rachael Wardell
turns.text: Coordination between health, education and children’s services, faster registration, workforce investment and targeted specialist provision are the priorities if we want better outcomes and value for money.

turns.speaker: Lucy Butler
turns.text: RCCs can make a difference for specialist supply and training but need time, funding confidence from councils, and national alignment where children cross regions.

turns.speaker: Gerald Vernon-Jackson
turns.text: We need honesty about scale and pace. RCCs, stricter market rules and more local capacity are parts of the answer, but expect slow progress without substantial funding and system changes.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you all for clear, practical evidence. Please send the data you offered on registration delays and costs.
